name: Attendance and Early Warning
title: Attendance and Early Warning
answer: Attendance and early warning means using attendance data and risk predictions to spot students who may be struggling, then having a person follow up with a conversation rather than a label. It matters because chronic absence is one of the clearest signs a student is in trouble, and data alone cannot reveal the reason or provide the help.

sections.body: This idea addresses the gap between noticing that a student is missing school and understanding why. Chronic absence is one of the clearest warning signs that a student is struggling, and early warning systems can predict who is at risk of failing or dropping out. But predictions and flags are only starting points, and the strongest approach pairs the data with a person who follows up. The problem it solves is that numbers alone cannot tell staff that a student is caring for a sick parent, being bullied, or missing the bus, and treating a flag as a fixed label can harm the student instead of helping.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a student information system flags students whose absences are rising, and then an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher follows up. That follow up might be a call home, a meeting, or a visit, and it is through that contact that the real reason for the absence comes to light. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the practice applies across year groups with the same principle: data raises the flag, a person has the conversation. Early warning systems work alongside this by predicting which students are at risk of failing or dropping out, with machine learning able to improve those predictions when staff have the expertise to use it well. Staff should be trained to treat every flag as a reason for a conversation rather than a judgment about who a student is.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this area with research evidence. Messages to parents about their child's absences reduce chronic absence, with effects of 10 to 15 percent in the original trials and smaller effects in newer ones run at scale (Rogers & Feller, 2018; Robinson et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2025). A meta analysis of 13 recent studies of attendance interventions found a small average effect, stronger when carried out within a single school (Li, 2026). On early warning systems, machine learning can improve predictions but takes expertise to use well, and results from systems whose reasoning is hidden can be read through staff members' existing biases (Soland et al., 2020). Interviews with students whose risk predictions were wrong found that the errors came from sudden life events, such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble (Hlosta et al., 2022).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Messaging helps, but it is only part of the answer, and predictions are wrong in ways that matter. Early warning flags should never follow a student as labels, and a flag is a reason for a conversation, not a judgment about who a student is. Staff should be trained to see flags this way, and students and families should never be told that a computer has decided a child is at risk. The decisions about what a flag means and what happens next stay with people, not with the system.
